I say: The foundational principle is that whatever separates from a living being is impure (najis). Excepted from this is the shorn hair of an animal whose meat is lawful to eat, whether it is hair, wool, fur, or feathers, for all of these are pure (tahir) by consensus. Similarly, hair that falls out on its own or is plucked is pure according to the soundest opinion. Also excepted is the hair of a human being, a limb severed from a human, and [the hair] of fish and locusts, and the placenta of a human. All of these are pure according to the school's (madhhab) opinion. What we have mentioned regarding hair is a branch derived from the school's position that hair becomes impure upon death.

BRANCH: On What Separates from the Interior of an Animal
This is of two types. The first is that which does not coagulate or transform internally but rather exudes gradually. The second is that which transforms and collects internally, then exits. The first type, such as saliva, tears, sweat, and nasal mucus, has the same ruling as the animal from which it exudes: if that animal is impure, it is impure; otherwise, it is pure. The second type, such as blood, urine, feces, dung, and vomit, is impure from all animals, meaning both from those whose meat is eaten and those whose meat is not eaten. We have one opinion (wajh) that the urine and dung of an animal whose meat is eaten are pure. This is one of the two sayings of Abu Sa'id al-Isfakhri among our companions, and it was chosen by al-Ruyani. It is also the school of Malik and Ahmad. However, the well-known position of our school is that they are impure.

Is this ruling of impurity applied to these excretions from the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him)? There are two opinions (wajhan). The majority (jumhur) say yes. Regarding the urine of fish and locusts, their blood and dung, the dung of animals without flowing blood, and blood that exudes from the liver and spleen, there are two opinions. The soundest is that they are impure.

As for milk, it is pure from an animal whose meat is eaten, by consensus. It is impure from an impure animal. It is pure from a human according to the soundest opinion, and it was said it is impure, but a child is raised on it out of necessity. As for milk from a non-human animal whose meat is not eaten, it is impure according to the soundest opinion. Al-Isfakhri said it is pure.

As for rennet (infaha), if it is taken from a lamb after its death, or after it has eaten something other than milk, it is impure without dispute. If it is taken from a slaughtered lamb before it has eaten anything other than milk, there are two opinions (wajhan). The soundest, which many have definitively stated, is that it is pure.

As for semen (mani), from a human it is pure. It was said there are two sayings on it. It was also said the two sayings apply specifically to a woman's semen. The first opinion is the school's position. However, if we say that the moisture of a woman's vagina is impure, then her semen becomes impure by contacting it, just as if a man urinates and does not wash his penis with water, his semen becomes impure by contacting the impure place. As for semen from a non-human, from a dog, pig, or their offspring, it is impure. From other animals, there are several opinions (awjuh). The soundest is that it is impure. The second is that it is pure. The third is that it is pure from an animal whose meat is eaten, and impure from others, like milk.

I say: The soundest opinion according to the verifying scholars and the majority is the second opinion. And Allah knows best.

As for eggs, they are pure from an animal whose meat is eaten. Regarding eggs from other animals, the same two opinions apply as for its semen. These two opinions also apply to silkworm eggs (bazr al-qazz), for they are the origin of the worm, like an egg. As for the silkworm itself, it is pure without dispute, like all other animals.

As for musk, it is pure. Regarding the musk sac (fa'rah) when it separates from the gazelle while it is alive, there are two opinions. The soundest is that it is pure, like a fetus. If it separates after the gazelle's death, it is impure according to the soundest opinion, like milk. There is an opinion that it is pure, like a hardened egg.

As for a plant that grows on manure (sirjin), the companions said it is not impure in itself, but it becomes impure by contacting the impurity. If it is washed, it becomes pure. If it produces ears of grain, the outer grains are pure.

I say: Pus is impure, and likewise the water of sores if it has changed [due to impurity]; otherwise, it is not impure according to the school. The smoke of an impure substance is impure in the soundest opinion, and this is mentioned in the chapter on what is disliked to wear. The moisture of a woman's vagina and the clinging blood (alaqah) are not impure in the soundest opinion, nor is the chewed flesh (mudghah) according to the soundest opinion. Bile is impure, and so is the contents of a camel's stomach.

As for the water that flows from the mouth of a sleeping person, al-Mutawalli said: if it has changed, it is impure; otherwise, it is pure. Someone else said: if it is from the soft palate (lahawat), it is pure; if from the stomach, it is impure. It is known to be from the soft palate if it stops when his sleep is prolonged. If there is doubt, the principle is that it is not impure, but caution is to wash it. If it is ruled impure and a person is afflicted by it frequently, then it appears it is treated like flea blood, urinary incontinence, and similar cases.

Al-Qadi Husayn, al-Mutawalli, al-Baghawi, and others said: If an animal eats a grain and then expels it intact, if its hardness remains such that it would grow if planted, then its substance is pure, but its exterior must be washed, because although it became its food, it did not change into corruption, so it is like a swallowed pit. If its hardness is gone, such that it would not grow, then it is impure in itself. Al-Mutawalli said: The dirt (wasakh) that separates from a human in a bath or elsewhere has the same ruling as his corpse. Likewise, dirt separating from any other animal has the ruling of its corpse. There is consideration in what he said. It should be pure definitively, like sweat. And Allah knows best.

CHAPTER: On Still Water (al-Ma' al-Rakid)
Know that still water is of two types: little and much. Much is two qullas, and little is less than that. Two qullas are equivalent to five water-skins. Regarding its measure in ratls, there are opinions (awjuh). The soundest, which is the explicit text (nass), is five hundred Baghdadi ratls. The second is six hundred, as stated by Abu Abdullah al-Zubayri and chosen by al-Qaffal and al-Ghazali. The third is one thousand ratls, as stated by Abu Zayd. The soundest opinion is that this measurement is an approximation, so a slight deficiency that does not cause a noticeable difference in the effect of a specific amount of changing substances is not harmful. The second opinion is that it is a precise limit, and any deficiency is harmful.

I say: The most famous opinion, based on the approximation, is that a deficiency of up to two ratls is excused. It was said three or similar, and it was said one hundred ratls. If an impurity falls into a small amount of water and one doubts whether it is two qullas or not, the one who is certain, as stated by the author of al-Hawi and others, is that it is impure, because the impurity is certain. Imam al-Haramayn had two probabilities. The chosen view, rather the correct one, is to definitively rule it pure, because the principle is its purity, and we doubt the presence of a defiling impurity. The presence of impurity does not necessitate defilement. The measure of two qullas by area is one and a quarter cubits (dhira') in length, width, and depth. And Allah knows best.

Then, a small amount of water becomes impure by contacting an effective impurity, whether it changes or not. As for a non-effective impurity, such as a corpse of an animal without flowing blood, an imperceptible impurity, or the lapping of a cat whose mouth was impure and then it disappeared and it is possible it became pure, it does not become impure according to the school, as previously mentioned in the first case. The latter two cases will follow, Allah willing. Al-Ruyani, one of our companions, chose the opinion that it only becomes impure by changing. The sound and well-known opinion is the first.

As for a large amount of water, it becomes impure by changing due to impurity, by consensus, whether the change is slight or great, and whether it changes in taste, color, or smell. All of this is agreed upon here, unlike what was previously mentioned regarding pure water. This applies whether the impurity is mixed in or adjacent. There is a rare opinion (wajh shadhdh) regarding an adjacent impurity that it does not make it impure.

As for when water smells due to a carcass thrown on the bank of a river, it does not become impure, because there is no contact. If a large amount of water contacts an impurity and does not change due to the smallness of the impurity and its being consumed, it does not become impure, and all of it can be used according to the soundest opinion. According to one opinion, the amount of the impurity remains [impure]. If it does not change because the impurity matches the water in its properties, then it is measured by what would differ, as previously mentioned in the chapter on pure water. If only part of it changes, the soundest opinion is that all the water becomes impure, and this is what is mentioned in al-Muhadhdhab and others. In one opinion, only the changed part becomes impure.

I say: The soundest opinion is what al-Qaffal, the author of al-Tatimma, and others said: that the changed part is like a solid impurity. If the remaining water is less than two qullas, it is impure; otherwise, it is pure. And Allah knows best.

Then, if the change in water caused by an impurity disappears by itself, it becomes pure according to the soundest opinion. Al-Isfakhri said it does not become pure, and this is rare. If the smell of the impurity is not present because musk was thrown into it, or its taste because vinegar was thrown in, or its color because saffron was thrown in, it does not become pure by consensus. If the change disappears by throwing in earth, there are two sayings. The more apparent of the two is that it does not become pure, due to doubt about the removal of the change. If the change disappears by gypsum, lime, or other things that do not overcome the property of the change, it is like earth according to the soundest opinion. It was said it is like musk. Then some said the dispute regarding earth applies only if the change was in smell. As for a change in color, earth definitely has no effect on it. The relied-upon principles are silent on this detail.

I say: Rather, al-Mahamili, al-Furani, and others explicitly stated that the dispute applies to changes in all three properties. I have clarified this in my commentary Sharh al-Muhadhdhab. And Allah knows best.

BRANCH: An impurity that is imperceptible to the eye, like a drop of wine or a small amount of urine that is not visible due to its smallness, or a fly that lands on an impurity and then flies away—does it make water and clothing impure like a perceptible impurity, or is it excused? There are seven approaches (turuq) on this. One: it is excused in both. Two: it is not excused in either. Three: there are two sayings regarding both. Four: it makes water impure, and there are two sayings regarding clothing. Five: it makes clothing impure, and there are two sayings regarding water. Six: it makes water impure but not clothing. Seven: the opposite. Al-Ghazali chose the opinion of excusing it in both. The apparent position of the school, according to the majority, is the opposite.

I say: The chosen opinion of a group of verifying scholars is what al-Ghazali chose, and it is the soundest. And Allah knows best.

BRANCH: If a small amount of impure water is increased (kuththira) until it reaches two qullas, consider: if it is increased with something other than water, it does not become pure. Rather, if pure water that is less than two qullas is completed with rose water, reaching two qullas, and the rose water is consumed [in the mixture], then if an impurity falls into it, it becomes impure, even if it does not change. This is because two qullas of pure water do not accept impurity. If it is increased with used water (musta'mal), it returns to being a purifier (mutahhir) according to the soundest opinion. According to the second opinion, it is like rose water. If it is increased with unused water, whether pure or impure, it returns to being a purifier without dispute. Is it a condition that there be no solid impurity in it? There is a far-fetched dispute on this. All of this applies if it reaches two qullas and does not change. If it is increased but does not reach two qullas, the soundest opinion is that it remains impure. The second opinion is that it is pure but not a purifier, with the conditions that the increasing substance is a purifier, that it is more than the water it is added to, that it is poured into the impure water, and that there is no solid impurity in it. If any of these conditions are violated, it is impure without dispute. None of these four conditions are required when it is increased to reach two qullas.

I say: What he has deemed sound is the soundest opinion. According to the Khurasanis, it is the soundest. The soundest opinion according to the Iraqis is the second. And Allah knows best.

What matters in increasing (mukathara) is the joining and combining, not the mixing. So if one of the two parts is clear and the other is cloudy, and they are joined, the impurity is removed without waiting for the mixing that prevents distinction. Whenever we rule purity in these cases, if it is then separated, it does not harm, and it remains a purifier.

BRANCH: If a solid impurity falls into a large amount of still water, there are two sayings. The more apparent of the two, which is the old saying (qadim), is that it is permissible to scoop from any place one wishes, and it is not obligatory to keep a distance, because all of it is pure. The second, the new saying (jadid), is that one must keep a distance from the impurity by the measure of two qullas. According to this, in the sea, keeping a distance of a span is not sufficient, considering the depth. Rather, one must keep a distance such that if the same measure were calculated in the depth and all other directions, it would amount to two qullas. If the water is spread out without depth, one keeps a distance in length and width that would amount to two qullas at that depth. Muhammad ibn Yahya said: in this case, one must keep a distance to a place where one knows the impurity has not spread. If the water is only two qullas, then according to the new saying, it is not permissible to scoop from it. According to the old saying, it is permissible in the soundest opinion. Then, in the first issue, it is possible that the dispute is about the permissibility of using the water without keeping a distance, while being certain that all of it is pure. It is also possible that the dispute is about its use, based on a dispute about its impurity. It has been reported from Shaykh Abu Muhammad that there is a consensus on the first possibility.

I say: This hesitation from Imam al-Rafi'i is strange, for a group of our senior companions have definitively stated and clarified the first possibility, including Shaykh Abu Hamid al-Isfarayini, al-Qadi Abu al-Tayyib, the author of al-Hawi, al-Mahamili, the authors of al-Shamil and al-Bayan, and others from the Iraqis and Khurasanis. A group of Khurasanis definitively stated, based on the saying of keeping a distance, that the avoided part is impure. This was stated by al-Qadi Husayn, Imam al-Haramayn, al-Baghawi, and others. These three even said: if the water was only two qullas, it would be impure according to this saying. The correct view is the first. And Allah knows best.

If a cup filled with impure water is immersed in a large amount of pure water, if it has a wide opening, the soundest opinion is that it returns to being a purifier. If it has a narrow opening, the soundest opinion is that it does not become pure. If we rule that it is a purifier in both cases, does this take effect immediately, or is a period of time necessary for the change to disappear if it was changed? There are two opinions (wajhan). The soundest is the second. The time required for the narrow opening is longer than for the wide one. If the water in the cup was changed, its change must disappear. If the cup was not full, then as long as water enters it, there is no connection, and it remains impure.

I say: Unless more water enters it than what is in it, in which case its ruling is what was previously mentioned regarding increasing (mukathara).

Al-Qadi Husayn and the author of al-Tatimma said: If the water in the cup was pure, and it is immersed in impure water that is less than two qullas by the amount of the cup's water, is the impure water ruled pure? There are the two opinions (wajhan) on this. And Allah knows best.

BRANCH: The water of a well is like other water in accepting impurity and its removal. If it is a small amount and becomes impure by an impurity falling into it, one should not bail it out so that pure water springs forth after it, because even if one bails it, the bottom of the well remains impure, and the walls of the well have also become impure by the bailing. Rather, one should leave it so it increases and reaches the limit of abundance. If its spring is weak and one does not expect it to increase, one should pour water into it to reach abundance, and the change should be removed if it was changed. The method of its removal is as previously mentioned, with its agreements and disputes. If the water is abundant and pure, and an impure thing disintegrates in it, like a mouse whose hair falls out, it may remain a purifier due to its abundance and lack of change, but its use becomes difficult, because no bucket is drawn without containing some of the impurity. Therefore, all the water should be drawn out to remove the hair. If the spring is gushing and drawing all the water is difficult, one should draw what one strongly suspects will remove all the hair. What remains in the well after that, and what springs forth, is a purifier, because its impurity is neither certain nor strongly suspected. The mere possibility of hair remaining is not harmful. If hair is confirmed after that, it is ruled upon accordingly. Before drawing to the mentioned limit, if one strongly suspects that every bucket contains some impurity, but is not certain, then the permissibility of its use is subject to the two sayings regarding the conflict between the principle and the apparent.

What we have mentioned regarding hair is a branch of its impurity upon death. If it is not ruled impure, then the issue is considered with other parts.

CHAPTER: On Flowing Water (al-Ma' al-Jari)
It is of two types: the water of moderate rivers and the water of great rivers. As for the first type, an impurity falling into it can be liquid or solid. The liquid impurity can be changing or non-changing. The changing one makes the changed part impure. The ruling of the rest of the water with it is like its ruling with a solid impurity. As for the non-changing liquid impurity, if the lack of change is due to matching the water in properties, its ruling is what was previously mentioned for still water. If it is due to the smallness of the impurity and its dissipation in the water, then the apparent position of the school and the saying of the majority is that it is like still water: if it is a small amount, it becomes impure; if it is a large amount, it does not. Al-Ghazali said it is pure absolutely. In the old saying, flowing water only becomes impure by changing.

I say: A group chose the opinion of purity, including Imam al-Haramayn and the author of al-Tahdhib. And Allah knows best.

As for a solid impurity, like a corpse, if it changes the water, it makes it impure. If it does not change it, then sometimes it stops and sometimes it flows with the water. If it flows with the current, then what is before it and what is after it are pure. What is to its right, left, above, and below, if it is a small amount, is impure. If it is two qullas, it was said it is pure, and it was said it is subject to the two sayings on keeping a distance. If the impurity stops and the water flows over it, its ruling is the ruling of the flowing impurity. Additionally, here, the water flowing over the impurity, if it is a small amount, becomes impure by contacting it, and it is not permissible to use it unless two qullas of it collect in one place. There is an opinion that if one keeps a distance and scoops from a place between which and the impurity there are two qullas, its use is permissible. The correct view is the first. Based on this, it is said: water that is a thousand qullas is impure without change. This is its example.

As for a great river, nothing is avoided in it, nor is there a "harim" (protected zone) of the impurity, and the dispute about keeping a distance from around the impurity does not apply. There is a rare opinion that it does apply. There is an opinion that one must avoid the harim specifically, and al-Ghazali definitively stated this, extending it to the harim of still water as well. The school's position is to definitively state that avoiding the harim is not obligatory in flowing or still water. Then, a "great" river is one where it is possible to keep a distance of two qullas from all sides of the impurity. A "moderate" river is one where this is not possible. An example of a moderate river is one whose banks are only two qullas apart. Imam al-Haramayn said: a moderate river is one that can be changed by customary impurities. A great river is one that cannot be changed by them. As for the harim, it is the area affected by the impurity through its movement, its turning, and its swirling around it.

I say: Liquids other than water become impure by contacting an impurity, no matter how abundant they are. Water alone is not made impure due to its strength. If one performs ablution from a well, then extracts a swollen chicken from it, he is not obliged to repeat any prayer except the one he is certain he prayed with the impure water. This was mentioned by the author of al-Uddah. And Allah knows best.

CHAPTER: On Removing Impurity (Izalat al-Najasah)
Impure things are of two types: impure in essence (najis al-ayn) and other than that. Impure in essence never becomes pure under any circumstances, except wine, which becomes pure by turning into vinegar, and the skin of a corpse, which becomes pure by tanning. Also excepted are the clinging blood (alaqah), the chewed flesh (mudghah), and the blood that is the filling of an egg, if we rule these three impure, they become pure if they transform into animals. As for that which is not impure in essence, it is of two types: tangible impurity (najasah ayniyyah) and ruling impurity (hukmiyyah). The ruling impurity is that whose existence is certain but is not perceived, like urine that has dried on a surface with no smell or trace. In this case, it is sufficient to pour water over the place once, and it is recommended to do so a second and third time. As for tangible impurity, one must attempt to remove whatever is present of its taste, color, and smell. If one does this and a taste remains, it is not pure. If only the color remains and it is easy to remove, it is not pure. If it is difficult to remove, like menstrual blood on a garment that may not go away even with excessive washing and the use of scraping and rubbing, it becomes pure. There is a rare opinion that it does not become pure. Scraping and rubbing are not conditions but are recommended according to the majority. It was said they are conditions. If only the smell remains and it is difficult to remove, like the smell of wine, there are two sayings, or two opinions. The more apparent is that it becomes pure. If both color and smell remain, it is not pure according to the soundest opinion. Then, the soundest opinion, which the majority stated, is that what we rule pure despite the remaining color or smell is truly pure. It is also possible that it is impure but excused. This was alluded to in al-Tatimma. Then, after the substance is removed, it is recommended to wash it a second and third time. Wringing the garment is not a condition for achieving purity in the soundest opinion, based on the purity of the washing water. If we adopt the weak opinion that wringing is a condition, then drying takes its place in the soundest opinion, because it is more effective in removing water.

BRANCH: What we mentioned about the place becoming pure with or without wringing applies when the water is poured onto the place. If the water is brought to the impure place, like a garment immersed in a basin of water and washed in it, there are two opinions. The soundest, stated by the majority, is that it does not become pure. Ibn Surayj said it does become pure. If the wind throws it into the water and the water is less than two qullas, the water also becomes impure without dispute.

BRANCH: If urine hits the ground and water is poured over it, covering and consuming it, the ground becomes pure after the water has dried up. Before it dries, there are two opinions. If we say wringing is not obligatory, it becomes pure. If we say it is obligatory, it does not become pure. Based on this, the ruling of purity does not depend on drying, but it is sufficient for the water to seep away, like a wrung garment. It is sufficient for the poured water to cover the impurity in the soundest opinion. It was said that it must be seven times the amount of urine. It was said that for the urine of one person, one bucket (dhanub) is required, for two people, two buckets, and so on. Then wine and all other liquid impurities are like urine; the ground is purified from them by covering with water without a specific measure, according to the school.

BRANCH: Impure milk is of two types: mixed with a solid impurity, like dung or bones of a corpse, and not mixed. The first type is impure with no way to purify it, due to the impurity's essence. If it is cooked, the school's position—which is the new saying—is that it remains impure. In the old saying, there is a statement that impure earth is purified by the removal of the impurity through sun, wind, and the passage of time. Abu Zayd, al-Khidri, and others derived from this a saying that fire has an effect, so its exterior becomes pure by cooking. According to the new saying, if it is washed, it does not become pure in the soundest, explicit-text opinion. Ibn al-Marzuban and al-Qaffal said its exterior becomes pure. As for the non-mixed type, like dough made with impure water or urine, its exterior becomes pure by pouring water over it, and its interior becomes pure by soaking it in water until it reaches all its parts, like dough made with an impure liquid. This applies if it has not been cooked. If it is cooked, it becomes pure—according to Abu Zayd's derivation—in its exterior, and likewise its interior in the more apparent opinion. According to the new saying, it remains impure, and washing purifies its exterior but not its interior. Its interior is only purified by pounding it into dust and then pouring water over it. If, after cooking, it is soft and does not prevent water from penetrating, it is as it was before cooking.

I say: If an impurity hits a polished object, like a sword, knife, or mirror, it is not purified by wiping according to us. Rather, it must be washed. If a knife is soaked in impure water and then washed, its exterior becomes pure. Are its interior parts purified by mere washing, or are they not purified until it is soaked a second time in purifying water? There are two opinions. If meat is cooked in impure water, its exterior and interior become impure. Regarding how to purify it, there are two opinions. One: it is washed and then wrung, like a carpet. The second: it must be boiled in purifying water. Al-Qadi Husayn and al-Mutawalli definitively stated in the two issues of the knife and the meat that it must be soaked a second time and boiled. Al-Shashi chose the sufficiency of washing, and this is the explicit text. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said in al-Umm, in the chapter on the prayer of fear: If one heats an iron and pours impure poison on it, or immerses it in it so it absorbs it, then washes it with water, it becomes pure, because all purifications are only for what is apparent, not for the interiors. This is his exact text. Al-Mutawalli said: If we require soaking the knife, it is permissible to cut moist things with it before soaking, just as one cuts dry things. If mercury is hit by an impurity, if it does not separate into pieces, it is purified by pouring water over it. If it separates, like oil, it cannot be purified in the soundest opinion. This was mentioned by al-Mahamili and al-Baghawi. Removing an impurity that one is not sinful for having on one's body is not obligatory immediately, but only when one intends to pray or similar acts. It is recommended to hasten it. Al-Mutawalli and others said: Water has strength when it encounters an impurity, so it does not become impure by contacting it, but remains a purifier. If one pours it on the place of impurity on a garment and the moisture spreads in the garment, the place of the moisture is not ruled impure. If one pours water into an impure vessel and it does not change due to the impurity, it is a purifier. If one swirls it around its sides, all the sides become pure. He said: If one washes a garment from an impurity, and another impurity falls on it right after wringing, is it obligatory to wash the entire garment, or is it sufficient to wash the place of the impurity? There are two opinions. The soundest is the second. And Allah knows best.

BRANCH: The obligatory method for removing impurity is washing, except for the urine of a male infant who has not eaten food and has only drunk milk. For this, sprinkling (nadh) is sufficient, provided the water reaches the entire area of the urine. Then, sprinkling has three degrees. The first: mere sprinkling. The second: sprinkling with abundance and force. The third: adding flow to it. There is no need for the third degree in sprinkling, definitively. The first degree is sufficient according to one opinion, but the second is needed in the soundest opinion. The urine of a female infant is not treated like that of a male infant; rather, washing is obligatory in the soundest opinion.

I say: In al-Tatimma, there is a rare opinion that a male infant is like a female infant, and washing is obligatory. Al-Baghawi said: The urine of a hermaphrodite (khuntha) is like that of a female, regardless of which of its two orifices it comes from. And Allah knows best.

CHAPTER: On the Purification of What a Dog Has Lapped
What a dog has lapped from, or what has become impure by its blood, urine, sweat, hair, or other parts and excretions, must be washed seven times, one of which is with earth. Regarding things other than lapping, there is a rare opinion that washing once is sufficient, like other impurities. The pig is like the dog in the new saying. In the old saying, washing once is sufficient, like other impurities. It was said the old saying is like the new saying. Soap, ash (ushnan), and similar substances do not take the place of earth in the most apparent opinion, like in tayammum. In the second [washing], it takes its place, like tanning and istinja'. In the third, if earth is available, it does not take its place; if not, it does. It was said it takes its place in what earth would spoil, like clothes, but not vessels. If one limits oneself to water and washes it eight times, there are opinions (awjuh). The soundest is that it does not become pure. The second is that it becomes pure. The third is that it becomes pure when earth is absent, but not when it is present. Immersing the vessel or garment in a large amount of water is not sufficient in the soundest opinion. Impure earth is not sufficient in the soundest opinion, like in tayammum. If an earthen ground is made impure by a dog's impurity, water alone is sufficient in the soundest opinion, as there is no meaning to dusting the earth with earth. For using earth, merely sprinkling it on the place is not sufficient. Rather, a liquid must be mixed with it so that the earth reaches all parts of the place through it. If the liquid is water, the purpose is achieved. If it is something else, like vinegar or rose water, and it is washed six times with water, it is not sufficient in the correct opinion, just as if the seven washes were done with vinegar and earth.

I say: If multiple dogs lapped in a vessel, or one dog lapped multiple times, there are three opinions. The correct one is that seven washes are sufficient for all. The second is that seven washes are obligatory for each lapping. The third is that seven washes are sufficient for the multiple lappings of one dog, but seven are obligatory for each dog.
